summary: Defines the Entity Attestation Token, an attested claims set describing the state and characteristics of an entity such as a phone, IoT device or network equipment. A relying party uses it to decide how much to trust the entity. It is carried as a CBOR Web Token or a JSON Web Token.

plainLanguage.summary: A device hands over a signed report card about itself, so someone can decide how far to trust it.

subtitle: A signed bundle of claims in which a device tells a server what it is, what software it runs, and what state it is in.

tldr.problem: A server often needs to decide how far to trust a device such as a phone, IoT sensor or router, and it needs a standard way for the device to describe its identity, software and state.
tldr.mechanism: An EAT is a claims set, carried as a CBOR Web Token (CWT) or JSON Web Token (JWT), made of attestation-oriented claims such as nonce, UEID, OEM ID, software name and debug status. Profiles pin down the options for a given use case.
tldr.outcome: A relying party can accept, refuse or partly trust an entity based on verified claims. EAT is a framework: the claims are standard, but how much each one can be trusted depends on the attester and the verifier.

today: RFC 9711 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2025, and no RFC obsoletes or updates it. The RFC leaves EAT media types to a separate document and says one basic profile for constrained devices is defined here, with other profiles expected for other use cases.

sections.title: What an Entity Attestation Token Is
sections.content:
An Entity Attestation Token (EAT) is a message made of claims about an entity, which can be a device, some hardware or some software. A relying party uses the claims to decide whether to trust the entity, not trust it, or trust it partially. The RFC's example of partial trust is allowing a money transaction only up to a limit. In EAT, an entity never means a person or organization.

EAT follows the operating model of the RATS architecture (RFC 9334). An attester produces evidence, a claims set that is usually signed and that includes a received nonce or uses another means to show freshness. A verifier checks the signature, may compare claims with reference values, and produces attestation results, which can also be an EAT. The relying party consumes the results. In some cases the verifier and relying party are not separate.

Attestation is not like server or user authentication. For attestation, keys belong to specific devices and are set up by device manufacturers. EAT is a framework for building tokens for specific use cases, not one fixed token.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a toy that can show a sealed note about who made it and how it is working, so the shop can decide whether to let it in.

sections.title: Token Structure: CWT, JWT and Claims-Sets
sections.content:
An EAT is an encoded message whose job is to move a Claims-Set between two parties. In this RFC an EAT is always a CWT or a JWT, so it gets authenticity and integrity protection from them, and EAT inherits their characteristics and security mechanisms. It is encoded in CBOR or JSON, and like CWT and JWT it implies no message flow. Other encodings and security mechanisms may be defined later.

Claims are defined once in CDDL and then encoded either way. A CBOR token must use only integer claim keys, and a JSON token must use only text claim names. All claims in a token must use the same encoding, with the exception of nested tokens. No claim is mandatory in general. Which claims a valid EAT needs depends on the context, and claims that an implementation does not understand MUST be ignored.

EAT keeps all the cryptographic flexibility of COSE and JOSE. It adds no new restrictions on algorithms, and a profile can narrow the choices.
sections.plainLanguage: The note can be written in a compact code or in plain words, but either way it is sealed, and the reader skips any line it does not understand.

sections.title: Claims That Describe the Entity
sections.content:
Claims in the entity section describe the entity itself, whether they appear in evidence or in attestation results. Key examples:

  • eat_nonce: a freshness value that MUST have at least 64 bits of entropy. In CBOR it is a byte string of 8 to 64 bytes, and an array of nonces is allowed.
  • ueid: a Universal Entity ID, like a serial number that is globally unique and permanent. Consumers MUST treat it as an opaque string of bytes. sueids are semipermanent versions that may change on life-cycle events such as a factory reset.
  • oemid: the hardware maker, as a 16-byte random number, an IEEE identifier or an IANA Private Enterprise Number. hwmodel and hwversion only appear alongside it.
  • swname and swversion: simple free-form software naming. For rigorous naming, manifests carries manifests such as CoSWID and measurements carries measurements taken on the entity. measres reports whether measurements matched reference values.
  • oemboot, dbgstat, uptime, bootcount, bootseed, location and dloas (Digital Letters of Approval, certifications the entity has received).

Two claims describe the token itself: iat (creation time, which must not be floating point) and eat_profile. The intuse claim says what the token is for.
sections.plainLanguage: The report card has lines for the serial number, the maker, the software on board and whether the back panel is open for fixing.

sections.title: Submodules, Nested Tokens and Detached Bundles
sections.content:
Complex devices such as phones have many subsystems. The submods claim lets claims for each subsystem be grouped. A submodule does not inherit anything from the token around it and must state every claim itself. The RFC specifically warns that a receiver MUST NOT assume debug is off in a submodule because the parent says so.

A submodule can take three forms:

  • a Claims-Set, secured by the same key as the enclosing token;
  • a nested token, a signed EAT from a subsystem that has its own keys, which cryptographically binds it to the outer token and may use a different encoding (a CWT inside a JWT, for example);
  • a detached submodule digest, which holds a hash algorithm identifier and a digest of a claims set that is sent separately.

A detached EAT bundle carries an EAT plus the detached claims sets it protects. The EAT must contain at least one detached digest and must be integrity protected. In CBOR a bundle can be identified with tag 602. If a detached claims set changes in transit, validation fails.
sections.plainLanguage: A big machine can attach a sealed note from each of its parts, so you know each part spoke for itself.

sections.title: Profiles and the Constrained Device Profile
sections.content:
CBOR, JSON, COSE and JOSE have many options, so two sides can both follow the standard and still fail to interoperate. EAT handles this with profiles: documents that fix the choices for one use case. A profile covers whether CBOR, JSON or both are sent, how arrays and strings are encoded, CBOR tags, signing, MAC and encryption formats, algorithms, key identification, freshness and which claims are required or forbidden. A full profile leaves no undecided options, and only full profiles may be named with the eat_profile claim. Profiles do not need to be on the Standards Track or registered anywhere.

The RFC defines one normative profile, the Constrained Device Standard Profile, identified as urn:ietf:rfc:rfc9711. It requires CBOR with definite-length maps, arrays and strings, preferred serialization, COSE_Sign1, and ES256, ES384 or ES512 signatures. Detached bundles are not allowed. The verification key is identified by the COSE kid or the UEID, and a new single unique nonce is required for every token request. Any deviation, even slight, needs a different profile identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: A profile is a rule sheet that says exactly which kind of note and which kind of seal to use, so both sides get it right.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
Some EAT claims can be used to track the owner of an entity, so implementations should consider privacy-preserving options. For example, the location claim might be left out of tokens sent to unauthenticated consumers.

A UEID is usually not privacy-preserving, because relying parties can recognize the same entity across tokens. Ways to include one anyway are to get explicit permission, to use it only in one context for one relying party, or to authenticate the relying party and derive a UEID just for it, for example by hashing. Geographic location is almost always personally identifiable information. The bootseed claim is effectively a stable identifier within a boot epoch, so it does not suit privacy-preserving schemes. A nonce derived from something like a username could also leak identity, so the RFC advises deriving it with a salt from a reliable random source.
sections.plainLanguage: Some lines on the report card, like a serial number or where you are, could be used to follow you around, so you should not always include them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of CWT, JWT and RFC 9334 apply to EAT. The RFC states that it defines what each claim means, not a required security level for the attester. The receiver learns how far to trust a claim by understanding the attester vendor's implementation and the checks the verifier made. For example, it says a UEID must be permanent but says nothing about defending against an attacker who changes it.

All EAT use MUST provide a freshness mechanism to prevent replay, and the EAT nonce is one option. Manufacturers should protect private key material before provisioning it into an entity. When several consumers are involved, exposure to each should be minimized, and claims passed downstream after COSE encryption is removed MUST be protected with an equivalent protocol such as TLS. A verification key must itself be established as trustworthy by some out-of-band mechanism, because key identification alone is never enough.
sections.plainLanguage: A fresh signed note proves it is new. But a signed note is only as honest as the device that wrote it, so you still have to judge who made it.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
EAT reuses the existing CWT and JWT claims registries and creates no new claim registry. The claims in this RFC were added to both. The CWT claim key for eat_nonce is 10, and the keys for the other new claims run from 256 (ueid) to 275 (intuse).

IANA also registered UEID URN subtypes, allocated CBOR tag 602 for the detached EAT bundle, and created an "Entity Attestation Token (EAT) Intended Uses" registry under Expert Review. Its initial values are 1 Generic, 2 Registration, 3 Provisioning, 4 Certificate Issuance and 5 Proof of Possession.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule book was added to the lists of known labels that everyone already uses, so nobody picks the same label twice.

items.desc: All debug facilities are permanently disabled.
